table_title: List the chemical elements first scientifically observed between 1869 (year of Mendeleev's periodic table publication) and 1945 (end of World War II) inclusive, with the year of first observation. (The universe is filtered by the source's 'Observed Year' column only; elements with Observed Year before 1869 but Isolated Year in 1869-1945 — e.g., Fluorine, Titanium, Cerium, Helium — are excluded.)
db_analog: SELECT element, observed_year FROM chemical_elements WHERE observed_year BETWEEN 1869 AND 1945 ORDER BY element
temporal_note: Wikipedia 'Discovery of the chemical elements' master article, accessed 2026-05-12 (re-validated 2026-05-12 during cycle-1 repair). Universe is the 31 chemical elements first scientifically observed between 1869 (Mendeleev's periodic table publication year) and 1945 (end of World War II) inclusive, as listed in the article's canonical chronological-discoveries wikitable (pandas.read_html identifies it as tables[4], 106 parsed rows total of which 104 are element-discovery rows and 2 are non-element historical-milestone rows — Lavoisier's 1789 'first modern list of chemical elements' entry and Mendeleev's 1869 periodic-table-arrangement entry, both with NaN Z and Element cells that the pipeline filter drops). The 31 staged rows are exactly the element-discovery rows with Observed Year in [1869, 1945]. Per-row cells: Element name verbatim from the source's Element column; Discovery Year is the 4-digit year of the source's 'Observed Year' column (the year of first scientific observation). The source's 'Isolated Year' column is NOT used as a fallback in this instance — 10 elements have Observed Year pre-1869 but Isolated Year in 1869-1945 (Fluorine Obs 1771/Iso 1886, Titanium 1791/1875, Cerium 1803/1875, Thorium 1829/1914, Lanthanum 1838/1904, Neodymium 1841/1901, Erbium 1843/1934, Terbium 1843/1937, Caesium 1860/1882, Helium 1868/1895); these are excluded by the strict Observed-Year-only filter. The universe-rule defensibility for this instance is the conventional chemistry-history 'discovery year' = first scientific observation, which is what the source's Observed Year column tracks. Discovery years span 1875 (Gallium, the first Mendeleev-predicted element discovered) to 1945 (Promethium, completing the rare-earth series). Underlying historical-record facts (which element was discovered in which year by whom) are stable on a multi-century horizon; the universe will only change if Wikipedia revises a discovery year (rare) or if the source restructures its tables.
_extraction_notes: Original instance filling the `factual_lookup` category gap (gap 4 → gap 3 after this staging — the category target was raised from 3 to 5 in the 2026-05-12 tier-simplification refresh, moving factual_lookup from gap 2 to gap 4). User-selected variant F from a slate of 6 factual_lookup #2 candidate angles. Source plan: Tier B Wikipedia, source_count = 1 — the master 'Discovery of the chemical elements' Wikipedia article supplies all per-row cells via its main chronological-discoveries wikitable (tables[4] per pandas.read_html). Pipeline: (1) fetch the cited Wikipedia article HTML, (2) parse with pandas.read_html identifying tables[4] (the canonical 106-parsed-row chronological-discoveries wikitable, of which 104 are element-discovery rows and 2 are non-element historical-milestone rows — Lavoisier 1789 and Mendeleev 1869 entries with NaN Z/Element cells; tables[0]-[3] are sidebar/legend/prehistoric-discoveries; tables[5+] are navigation/index tables), (3) drop the 2 non-element rows via dropna(subset=['Year','Z']) which removes any row missing either Z or a parsed Year, (4) for each remaining row, extract Element name verbatim and derive Discovery Year as the 4-digit year from the 'Observed Year' column (regex '(\d{4})' captures the year cleanly), (5) filter to Observed Year ∈ [1869, 1945] inclusive (cycle-1 audit clarification: the Isolated Year column is NOT used as a fallback for this instance; the staged universe-rule is strictly Observed-Year-based to match the chemistry-history 'discovery year' convention), (6) sort alphabetically by Element. Result: 31 rows × 2 columns, PK on Element, 0 duplicates. The 31-row universe matches the strict 1869-1945 filter: Gallium 1875 is the first element in the window (Mendeleev predicted Gallium's existence in 1871 and Boisbaudran discovered it in 1875, validating the periodic table); Curium 1944 and Americium 1944 are among the latest (Manhattan Project transuranium discoveries); Promethium 1945 (last in window — completes the rare-earth series). Window-boundary notes: the lower bound 1869 is the year of Mendeleev's periodic table publication itself (no element discoveries in 1869-1874 within this window); the upper bound 1945 includes Promethium's 1945 discovery but excludes post-WWII discoveries (Berkelium 1949, Californium 1950, Einsteinium 1952, etc.). Confidence gradient is real and category-appropriate (factual_lookup tests single-attribute recall): very-LLM-knowable cells include the noble gases (Argon 1894, Neon/Krypton/Xenon 1898 — well-known Ramsay/Travers discoveries) and the radioactive trio (Polonium/Radium 1898 — Curies); mid-difficulty cells include the Mendeleev-predicted trio (Gallium 1875, Scandium 1879, Germanium 1886 — famously validated his periodic table); harder calibration cells include the rare-earth lanthanides (Praseodymium 1885, Europium 1896, Gadolinium 1880, Dysprosium 1886, Holmium 1878, Thulium 1879, Ytterbium 1878, Lutetium 1906) which test detailed chemistry-history knowledge; and the transuranium-era discoveries (Technetium 1937, Francium 1939, Astatine 1940, Neptunium 1940, Plutonium 1941, Americium/Curium 1944, Promethium 1945) which test 20th-century radiochemistry-program knowledge.
